newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMI president lavishes praise on BoE independence.
newsitem.headline: EMI president lavishes praise on BoE independence.

text.p: Britain's decision to give the Bank of England greater independence in setting monetary policy was greeted with enthusiasm on Wednesday by Alexandre Lamfalussy, head of the European Monetary Institute.
"It was music to my ears," Lamfalussy told a monetary sub-committee of the European Parliament.

The decision on Tuesday by Gordon Brown, Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer, to give the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates stunned financial markets and fuelled speculation that the new Labour government would be more sympathetic to the EU's planned single currency.
EU monetary officials praised the decision, with many calling it a step in the right direction.
But since Britain's Treasury still retains the right to set an inflation target for the central bank, the decision falls short of the Maastricht treaty's requirement of full autonomy.

"Maastricht or no Maastricht it's a good thing. I think this is a very major step towards compliance with the treaty's objectives," Lamfalussy said, adding the new policy would likely lead to greater stability for sterling.

Although Labour's stance towards economic and monetary union (EMU) is similar to that of the battered Conservative party -- both have taken a wait-and-see approach -- expectations in Brussels are that it will be a more cooperative partner.

Britain, which secured an opt-out to EMU during the Maastricht treaty's negotiations, would have to overcome several hurdles should it want to be considered for membership in the euro, due to start in 1999.
Foremost, it would have to re-join Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a complex grid that links virtually all of the EU's currencies in relatively wide trading bands.
This is a path which no one in Britain seems ready to go down.

Since its humiliating exit from the ERM in September 1992, British politicians have been loathe to reconsider a return to a regime which many believe would constrain economic growth and foster renewed currency turbulence.

Yet under the planned single currency, a new exchange system, dubbed ERM2, would link the euro to those currencies not joining in 1999. Since Britain is unlikely to join in time, speculation is growing over whether the more pro-European Labour government would eventually abandon the old policy.
The former ruling Conservatives argued forcefully and won a concession from its EU partners that membership in a new ERM should be non-complusory for countries outside monetary union.

Lamfalussy, while acknowleding Britain's fierce independence, nonetheless underscored the fact that it too had accepted a committment to future exchange rate stability once the single currency was launched.

Tuesday's decision to put the Bank of England on a more equal footing with other European central banks would only faciliate the much desired goal of currency stability throughout the continent, he added.
"I think the risks of having problems with the UK are substantially diminished," he added.

The EMI president also urged swift appointment of the executive board of a future European Central Bank and warned that the overhaul of social security systems within the EU posed one of the greatest challenges in preparing for the euro.
